title: 'Defying Gravity': IMF Says Global Economy Resists Chaos, but the Cushion Is Thinning
excerpt: Growth is projected at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027 despite wars and an energy shock, but emergency oil stocks are depleted and budgets overstretched.
body:
• The IMF projects global growth of 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, holding up through wars, an energy shock and trade conflict that historically would have tipped the world into crisis.
  • The cushion is thinning: the IEA ordered its biggest-ever emergency oil release in March, the US strategic reserve sits at its lowest since 1982, and government budgets are overstretched.
  • Headline inflation is projected at 4.7% in 2026, easing to 4.1% in 2027, driven by food and energy costs.
  • The split is widening: economies tied to the AI investment boom are holding up, while energy importers with little tech exposure face higher import bills, weaker currencies and shrinking fiscal space.

Inside Bangkok's Queen Sirikit conference centre this week, policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered for the IMF's annual meeting and contemplated an economy that, by historical standards, should be in crisis and is not, The Guardian reported via WCCPress. Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared.

The IMF's Numbers

The Fund's October World Economic Outlook projects growth of 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, with headline inflation at 4.7% this year easing to 4.1% next, according to Devdiscourse. Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva summarised the outlook in one line: the global economy has proved resilient, but "increasingly uneven and fragile."

"Global economic activity has proven resilient once again. In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events."

— IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026

The outlook, quoted by Left Horizons, lists the sequence: the pandemic and supply-chain disruption, wars in Ukraine and the Middle East with sharp energy price rises, and significant changes in trade barriers. Labour markets have stayed unexpectedly strong and inflation has receded from its peaks, though it remains persistent in several economies.

Why Gravity Has Not Bitten Yet

The IMF credits two shock absorbers. First, energy adjusted: supplies were rerouted around the Strait of Hormuz, production rose elsewhere, inventories were drawn down, and substitution and efficiency gains cushioned the oil disruption. Without those margins, the Fund says, the oil shock alone would have significantly reduced global growth in 2026. Second, the AI-driven investment boom lifted activity and trade, with investment rising on expected returns.

Why the Cushion Is Thinning

Both absorbers are finite. The International Energy Agency ordered its biggest-ever release of emergency stocks in March and later accelerated it; the US strategic reserve has been reported at its lowest point since 1982. Governments, meanwhile, are carrying heavy debts and deficits, leaving less room to shield households from a fresh price surge. Guardian columnist Larry Elliott called the moment "a crisis postponed rather than a crisis permanently avoided, a lull before the storm, in all probability."

What It Means for Portfolios

The Fund's own prescription is fiscal repair while growth holds: rebuild fiscal space, strengthen energy security and improve AI readiness. For investors, the split in the outlook is the actionable part. Economies integrated into the technology supply chain are strengthening; energy-importing economies outside it face compounding strain. Resilience, on the IMF's own telling, is a wasting asset.
